Clinical features include severe haemolytic anaemia, jaundice, pul- monary oedema, and renal failure. There is no established specific treatment for babesiosis. Treatment is not recommended for asymptomatic patients although all symptomatic patients should be treated with antibacterials to prevent the development of complica- tions.1 For serious infections, supportive therapies include red blood cell exchange transfusions to reduce parasitae- mia. Clindamycin with quinine was the first regimen used4 for the treatment of B. microti infections, but has been as- sociated with significant toxicity. A prospective ran- domised study5 in 58 patients found azithromycin with atovaquone to be as effective as clindamycin and quinine and associated with less toxicity. Azithromycin with qui- nine has been reported to be effective in 2 patients who had not responded to quinine plus clindamycin.6,7 Pentamidine has also been reported to produce clinical improvement in patients with B. microti infection,8 but the efficacy and safety of pentamidine has been questioned.9 Other drugs that have been tried with variable results include chloro- quine, primaquine, pyrimethamine, sulfadiazine, and tetra- cycline.2,3 The Infectious Diseases Society of America1 recommends a combination of either clindamycin plus quinine or atovaquone plus azithromycin, both orally for 7 to 10 days; the combination of intravenous clindamycin plus oral quinine should be used in severe babesiosis. In immunocompromised patients higher doses of azithromy- cin may be used; they are prone to relapsing disease, and treatment should be given for 6 weeks or more, including 2 weeks after parasites are no longer detectable in blood smears.10 Partial or complete exchange transfusion may also be given. Patients with persistent infection should be re-treated. Patients co-infected or suspected to be co-infected with Anaplasma phagocytophilum and/or Borrelia burgdorferi should also be given doxycycline for 10 days.1,3 For infor- mation on the treatment of co-infected patients see Lyme Disease, p.177. In B. divergens infections, treatment is complicated by the rapid progression of the disease. Anti- protozoal and antimalarial drugs have been tried with lim- ited success, although pentamidine with co-trimoxazole was successful in a patient,11 and a marked reduction in parasite load was seen in a patient treated with pentami- dine plus exchange transfusions.12 The combination of clindamycin plus quinine with exchange transfusion has also been suggested.2 Preventive measures against babesiosis include the use of tick repellents, physical protection, and prompt removal of attached ticks.1 1.
